speaker: jessieallen
text: Afternoon, and may it please the court. My name is Jesse Allen, and I'm here today on behalf of the Dallas County District Attorney's Office representing the state of Texas. The state respectfully asked this court to reverse the trial court's order suppressing the chemical analysis of Appalee's blood in this driving while intoxicated case, because the trial court mistakenly concluded that the state had to complete post-seizure chemical analysis of that blood within three days from the issuance of the warrant exclusive of the day of the issuance. Now, the general rule for a search warrant is that it must be executed within three days after it's issued. But Chapter 18 of the Code of Criminal Procedure does not specifically describe what actions a peace officer must take before the expiration of that time. Now, after both parties submitted their briefs in this case, this court issued its July 9th opinion in State v. Jones. And after this case was set for submission, the court granted the state's motion to publish that opinion. Jones resolves the issue in this case. The appellant in Jones argued that because this court's decision in State v. Staten allegedly merged the requirements to justify blood analysis with the requirements for obtaining a blood warrant, that the timeframe requirements for testing blood are controlled by the timeframe requirements for blood draws. In other words, the same argument that was made here, that 1807A3 controls analysis, not just seizure. Now, this court rejected that argument and plainly held that Article 1807A3 provides the deadlines for seizing evidence and not analyzing it. And that the execution of the warrant is the blood draw, not the testing or analysis of that blood. In this case, the police executed the warrant timely by seizing the appellee's blood on the same day that the magistrate issued the warrant. Now, this court's holding in Jones makes sense because the provisions of Chapter 18 governing search warrants suggest that a search and seizure warrant issued under that chapter is executed at the latest when the target item in the warrant is seized. Article 1801 of the Code of Criminal Procedure defines a search warrant as a written order issued by a magistrate and directed to a peace officer, commanding him to search for any property or thing and to seize the same. Article 1806, which is the only expressly titled provision in Chapter 18 dealing with execution of a warrant, has various provisions of it that clearly indicate that when we're talking about executing warrants, we're talking about seizing property. It says that the officer before taking property from a place must prepare a written inventory of the property to be taken. He has to endorse his name on that inventory and present it to the owner or other person who is in possession of that property. And if no one is there who is in possession of the property, he leaves it there at the place from where the items were seized. So the warrant, at least according to 1806, is executed by searching for and seizing the property to be taken. And seizure in the context of property means restraint of that property, or it includes the collection of the property and taking possession of it, according to Article 1809. Nothing in the description of how warrants are supposed to be executed in Chapter 18 aligns with the appellee's position at trial that testing for blood alcohol is part of the execution of a DWI blood draw warrant that commands the seizure of a blood specimen. Intangible results are not the item named in the warrant, the blood is. And test results are not taken from the place to be searched, the blood is. Now, in the court below, the appellee cited two provisions of 1807 that deal with varying amounts of time to execute search and seizure warrants under Chapter 18. The first was 1807A1, which deals with obtaining specimens for DNA analysis and comparison. That provision provides that the period allowed for execution of warrant is 15 days if the warrant is issued solely to search for and seize specimens from a specific person for DNA analysis and comparison, including blood and saliva samples. And that's our position that that provision is clear, it's not ambiguous, it's clearly talking about an execution time for obtaining the specimen. But if for whatever reason, someone could say that language is ambiguous and that the language talking about for DNA analysis and comparison somehow incorporated the testing phase of that evidence analysis into the execution. The statement of the bill sponsor, which we put in our brief cleared that up. The bill author slash sponsor was clearly concerned with individuals evading the police so the police couldn't get a sample at all. And it amended the law to provide for execution of the warrant to obtain the specimen and not to test that specimen. The other provision that was cited in the court below deals with data and information on devices, various storage devices that contain electronic data or information. And that provision provides that if a warrant is issued to search for or seize data or information contained in or on one of various listed storage devices, the warrant is considered to have been executed at the time the device was seized before the expiration of the time allowed. That provision does not, and it's important I think to note, that provision does not extend the time to execute the warrant. It's very likely that, well, it is the case that those are gonna fall under the general provision of 1807A, which is the three-day provision. It doesn't extend that time. It simply defines when seizure occurs. And it occurs when the tangible item that houses that intangible data is seized.
